title: Instinct
summary: Instinct Instinct is a personal assistant that understands what you're working on and what's important to you. The interface is simple: there are no new interfaces. You can text or call it. payload.text: Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot , a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers. Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo) Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders. Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away , Clare V. , Monica + Andy , Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers . The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive , Meta and Google , then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. In one case, Herrin described how Marklo identified a color trending on social media and a matching handbag a retailer had in stock but hadn’t promoted recently. It offered to plan a post based on one that had performed well before. Latico Leathers offers another example of how a brand uses Marklo. The company used the software to plan a month’s worth of marketing in one day, a process that had previously taken most of a week across meetings, spreadsheets and five tools, according to Herrin. In the end, humans review and approve Marklo’s proposed work. The company says it does not use customer data to train AI models. As for its revenue model, Marklo plans to charge a monthly subscription fee, with additional charges based on usage. For now, brands can install and try it for free. “I’m very passionate about small and medium businesses, and I want to make it accessible to every single brand that runs on Shopify,” Herrin told Crunchbase News in an interview, “so that they can operate like a big brand.” A change of direction The decision to build Marklo followed a change in how Herrin thought about Stella & Dot’s future. That company began as a way for women to earn money on their own schedules by hosting trunk shows in their own homes. It expanded into apparel and skincare and paid out more than $500 million to its sellers, Herrin said. “For me, it was never about the jewelry,” she told Crunchbase News. When COVID-19 put a stop to in-home gatherings, business dropped 80% almost overnight. Herrin also realized that women who might once have signed up to sell Stella & Dot products suddenly had other options. They could promote multiple brands as influencers or open their own Shopify stores. She described Stella & Dot as “the COVID victim that had pre-existing conditions.” Rather than rebuild the old model, Herrin sold the businesses and brands separately. Later, she bought back the Stella & Dot brand to sell through a different channel and test Marklo. She was also reconsidering what she wanted to do next. As she approached her 50th birthday, Herrin questioned whether she would choose to start the same business again. “As an entrepreneur, you don’t just start a business; you start a life,” she said. She still wanted to help people build businesses. What had changed was the problem she wanted to solve: Opening an online store had become easier, but managing its marketing still meant gathering information from several systems and coordinating the next campaign. “The mission was the same, but the solution needed to evolve,” Herrin said. A return to venture capital For Marklo, Herrin also returned to venture funding after relying more on profits to grow Stella & Dot. She had raised venture capital for her first company, which became WeddingChannel.com , but came away feeling that it had raised too much money. She took a different approach with Stella & Dot, building it with about $2 million in capital and a focus on profitability. “Here’s a new growth strategy,” Herrin recalled thinking. “How about profits?” With Marklo, she wanted to hire engineers and develop the software faster. Its 11-person team includes engineers who previously worked at Shopify and Google. She also sought investors with commerce experience. “Raising capital isn’t just about having money for expenses,” Herrin said. “It’s about bringing a brain trust together.” Experience as ‘the customer she’s building for’ Kirsten Green , founder and managing partner of Forerunner Ventures, said Herrin’s experience building Stella & Dot was a central reason for backing Marklo. “Jessica uniquely has been the customer that she’s building for right now at every stage, from starting a brand to having a brand at scale,” Green told Crunchbase News in an interview. That experience gives Herrin firsthand knowledge of where teams lose time, which decisions affect profitability and what brands need before trusting new technology, she added. While AI in general makes it easier to produce marketing content, Green sees the greater opportunity in helping brands decide on what exactly to promote, as well as in understanding the impact on margins and how to grow in ways consistent with their identity. Marklo, she said, incorporates the judgment needed to turn business data into useful recommendations. The opportunity comes as AI is taking a larger share of investment in the broader sales and marketing sector . Startups in sales, marketing and customer relationship management raised $7.5 billion across 830 rounds globally this year through mid-September, with most of that investment going to companies in Crunchbase’s AI-related categories. Funding is on pace to finish below 2025’s $11.1 billion, while deal volume could fall for a fourth straight year — a sign that investors are concentrating their bets in fewer companies. “It’s one thing to collect the information; it’s another thing to understand how to present it and how to recommend an action against it,” Green added. The investor also pointed to Marklo’s ability to serve businesses at different stages, noting that coordination becomes more complex and information harder to share as brands grow. As such, the prospect of software that can grow alongside its customers was another draw. Green said she also valued Herrin’s decision to develop Marklo alongside brands already using it, giving the company customer feedback before its broader launch. “I like the fact that she built this product while it was being used,” she said. title: How I Learned That Some Startup Problems Are Too Big For A Minimum Viable Product

payload.text: By Daniel Kjellén A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary. Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause. For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on. Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda. After selling my first venture, Tink , to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing. Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours. A problem with too many heads Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another. Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget. “Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one. Why the second time is different In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder. The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you. Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it. Maximum viable product Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink. We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs. You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet. Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda , the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022. payload.text: A total of 38 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in September, adding $71 billion in value to the board. Semiconductors, financial services and space technology led for new counts with the remainder hailing from a broad swath of industries including biotech, AI infrastructure, AI training, security and frontier labs. Twenty-one of last month’s new unicorns are U.S. headquartered. Six new unicorns joined the board from China and three from the U.K., while Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Israel, Italy, Finland, Germany and Bulgaria each added one new unicorn. Through September, 311 companies have joined the board so far this year, putting 2026 on track to be the second-highest year for new unicorn creation, following only the venture peak year of 2021, when counts topped 600. Several companies already on the board stand out for significant valuation increases via new raises last month. They include San Francisco-based Cognition , developer of AI for software engineering, which saw its value climb to $48 billion, up from $26 billion only four months earlier. Data center provider Crusoe was valued at $31 billion last month, up from $10 billion a year ago. And Paris-based frontier lab Mistral was valued at $24.4 billion in its more recent funding, up from $13.7 billion a year ago. New unicorns in September Here are September’s 38 new unicorn companies: Semiconductors Fab2 , an Austin-based semiconductor manufacturing startup, closed a $500 million Series A at a $3.7 billion valuation, led by Fundomo . The 3-year-old company builds compact chip factories and develops their manufacturing equipment internally, aiming to make semiconductor production more accessible. Celero Communications , an Irvine, California-based semiconductor company, raised a $275 million Series C, valuing it above $3 billion and bringing total funding to $415 million. Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners and CapitalG led the round. The 2-year-old company develops digital signal processing chips for high-speed optical connectivity in AI infrastructure. Micronano Core , a Hangzhou-based AI chip developer, announced a $149 million Series C. Its IoT inference chips combine memory and computing to reduce power consumption and data movement. The 5-year-old company was valued at $1 billion. Evas Intelligence , a Beijing-based AI chip company, raised $298 million at a valuation of $2.2 billion. The 4-year-old company develops AI computing chips using the open RISC-V architecture. SiMa.ai , a San Jose, California-based developer of specialized AI chips and software, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, co-led by Fidelity and Amplify Partners , bringing total funding to $500 million. The proceeds for the 8-year-old company will support its software platform and next-generation hardware for robots, vehicles and drones. Financial services OG , a Texas-based prediction-market platform, announced a strategic partnership with Robinhood , which will take an equity stake following OG’s separation from Crypto.com . The less than 1-year-old company was valued at $5 billion. The investment amount was not disclosed; the partnership will route Robinhood event-contract trading through OG’s regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure. Saudi Arabia-based Barq , a digital payments company, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion valuation. Investors included Noon Investments , Sohar International and M20 Capital . The 3-year-old company has processed more than $117 billion in 2 years. Ridgeline , a Nevada-based financial software company, raised a $250 million Series E at a $1.43 billion valuation led by founder and chairman Dave Duffield . The 8-year-old company provides an AI-based investment management platform for asset and wealth managers. Félix , a Miami-based remittance platform for Latino immigrants operating through WhatsApp , secured $200 million in financing: an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz valued at $1.4 billion and $113 million in debt from General Catalyst ’s Customer Value Fund. The 5-year-old company plans to expand to lending and add to its Latin American reach . Space technology Munich-based space company The Exploration Co. raised a $450 million Series C, co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners , Atomico and EQT at a valuation of $2 billion. The financing for the 5-year-old company will advance its reusable Nyx spacecraft for an International Space Station mission and support development of its Storm rocket engine. Hubble Network , a Seattle-based satellite connectivity company, raised a $200 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Smith Point Capital , bringing total funding to approximately $300 million. The 5-year-old company enables standard Bluetooth devices to connect directly to satellites for tracking and sensor-data applications. Oxfordshire, U.K-based Open Cosmos , a satellite company, secured $346 million, co-led by ETF Partners and Lightrock , valued at $1 billion. The 11-year-old company manufactures satellites and provides infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation and intelligence services. Bulgaria-based EnduroSat , a satellite company, raised $205 million in a round co-led by Riot Ventures and Atreides Management , reaching a $1 billion valuation. The 11-year-old company has raised financing that will expand standardized spacecraft production, including new manufacturing capacity in the U.S. and Europe. Biotechnology and medical devices Alzheon , a Framingham, Massachusetts-based developer of treatments for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders, raised around $79 million. The   13-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. Investors were not disclosed. Shanghai-based Anew Labs , an AI drug discovery company, raised $290 million at a $1.5 billion valuation following its spinoff from ByteDance . HSG , IDG Capital , Hillhouse Capital and 5Y Capital co-led the round. Anew develops tools for biomolecular prediction and drug discovery; ByteDance retained a 56% stake. Precision Neuroscience , a New York-based brain-computer interface developer, closed a $250 million Series D, bringing total funding to $430 million and reaching a valuation of approximately $1 billion. Pershing Square and Ackman Oxman Institute led the round. The 5-year-old company is building a brain–computer interface that is minimally invasive and removable. Toronto-based Biossil , a biotechnology company, raised $153 million at a $1 billion valuation led by the OpenAI Startup Fund , with participation from Founders Fund and other investors. The 3-year-old company uses AI to identify abandoned drug candidates that could succeed under different treatment approaches. The financing will expand clinical development and support additional drug acquisitions. AI and internet infrastructure Gimlet Labs , a San Francisco-based AI cloud infrastructure company, raised a $300 million Series B at a $3 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz . The 3-year-old company distributes AI inference workloads across different types of chips to improve performance and efficiency. It announced in March that its customers include one of the leading frontier labs. Helsinki-based Verda , an AI cloud company, raised a $189 million Series B led by Emergence Capital . The financing valued the 6-year-old company above $1 billion with total funding over $450 million. The company manages physical data centers along with its cloud platform. London-based CDN77 , an internet infrastructure company supporting content delivery for large streaming, gaming and software companies, raised $570 million in its first external financing led by CVC Capital Partners . The 15-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. AI training Micro1 , a San Francisco-based AI training-data company, raised more than $100 million led by Dream Ventures at a $4 billion valuation, an eightfold increase from its valuation in September 2025. The 4-year-old company recruits and vets specialists who create training and evaluation data for AI developers. Forbes reported that participants included two frontier AI laboratories and two x.AI co-founders. AfterQuery , a San Francisco-based provider of expert-created AI training data, reached a $3.2 billion valuation in September, more than 10x its valuation five months earlier, according to Forbes . The funding amount and lead investor were not publicly disclosed. The 1-year-old company’s datasets capture professional reasoning in fields such as software engineering, law and finance. AfterQuery was part of the Winter 2025 Y Combinator batch. Robotics and autonomous driving Shanghai Zaofu Intelligent Technology , the Shanghai-based operator of Hello’s robotaxi business, raised about $100 million at a valuation close to $3 billion. Shanghai State-owned Capital Investment fund led the round. The financing to the 1-year-old company will support a 10,000-GPU computing cluster, AI model development and commercialization of Level 4 autonomous driving. Lyte AI , a Sunnyvale, California-based robotics perception company, raised a $165 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Maverick Silicon . Founded by former Apple and PrimeSense engineers, the 5-year-old company combines custom chips, sensors and spatial software to help robots perceive their surroundings. The financing will accelerate deployments across logistics, manufacturing and inspection applications. Health insurance Angle Health , a San Francisco-based health benefits company, announced a $200 million Series C at a $2.7 billion valuation. Vitruvian Partners led the financing. It also includes $400 million in secondary financing for existing investors. The 7-year-old company provides a benefits platform using AI to make healthcare more affordable for small and midsize employers. The company services 5,000 businesses. Thatch , a San Francisco-based health benefits platform, raised a $108 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included The General Partnership , Index Ventures , General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz . The 5-year-old company helps employers provide individualized health budgets for employees to select their own medical plans. It has 5,000 employers utilizing its service. Energy and EV infrastructure China-based NIO Power , a battery-swapping and charging company, agreed to a strategic transaction that gives Geely Auto a 30% stake. Geely will contribute its Yiyi battery-swapping operation and a $95 million investment. The 9-year-old company was valued around $2.4 billion. TAR , an Austin-based developer of off-grid power systems for AI data centers, raised a $120 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation, led by Spark Capital . The less than 1-year-old company builds modular systems for renewable energy and battery systems as data-center operators seek access to electricity. AI applications Brahma AI raised $150 million led by Multiples , at a valuation just over $2 billion. The 3-year-old company, headquartered in London with offices in Los Angeles and Mumbai, built an enterprise audiovisual content platform for media, advertising, sports and healthcare customers. The financing will support research, commercial expansion and a larger Silicon Valley presence. Sequen , a New York-based AI ranking and personalization company, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.44 billion valuation, led by Prysm Capital . The 2-year-old company’s software helps enterprises respond to customer behavior in real time, improving the relevance of recommendations. Cybersecurity Rome-based Exein , a cybersecurity company protecting connected devices and autonomous machines, raised $270 million at a $1.7 billion valuation, led by Headline . The financing to the 8-year-old company will support U.S. and Asia-Pacific expansion and development of AI security models. Tel Aviv-based Guardio , a consumer cybersecurity company, raised $40 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $167 million. Wiz co-founder Assaf Rappaport joined existing investors including Ion Crossover Partners and Union Tech Ventures , among others. The 8-year-old company protects consumers against phishing, scams, malicious websites and AI-generated fraud. AI models Beijing-based Naive AI , a language-model startup, raised $120 million reaching a valuation of $1.4 billion. Investors include Tencent , IDG Capital , Matrix Partners China and HSG . The less than 1-year-old company raised $400 million across three rounds so far this year, before releasing its first public model. Arcee AI , a San Francisco-based developer of open-weight foundation models, announced a $150 million Series B led by Vista Equity Partners , Cambium Capital Partners and Emergence Capital , valuing the company above $1 billion. The financing will support the 3-year-old company’s Trinity models and products for customizing and operating them. Manufacturing and construction software CADDi , an AI company for manufacturing with dual headquarters in Tokyo and Chicago, raised a $114 million Series D at a $1.2 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $234 million. Investors included Moore Strategic Ventures and Coreline Ventures . The 9-year-old company’s platform organizes design and procurement and production; the financing will deepen its technology and accelerate North American expansion. Kahua , a Georgia-based construction software company, secured a growth investment of $250 million led by Bain Capital Tech Opportunities , valuing it above $1 billion. The 17-year-old company manages construction projects, with the investment supporting its AI capability build out and commercial growth. Defense technology Covenant , a Washington, D.C.-based defense company, emerged from stealth with $250 million raised across three rounds at a valuation above $1 billion. The 2-year-old company develops long-range cruise missiles with manufacturing in Texas, Germany and Israel. Backers who have led across three rounds include Andreessen Horowitz , Founders Fund , Lux Capital , 8VC 1 , Lightspeed Venture Partners and Aleph . Food Medici Brands , the New York-based parent of consumer food brands David Protein and HallPass, raised a $250 million Series B at a $2.25 billion valuation. Greenoaks and Valor Equity Partners co-led the round. The financing to the 2-year-old company will expand retail distribution, develop new products and support additional brands. payload.text: By Nnamdi Okike You have likely never heard of Tosin Eniolorunda . You should have. Over the past decade, Tosin and his team built Moniepoint into the operating system for more than 6 million Nigerian businesses, processing over $300 billion a year , or 39% of Nigeria’s digital payments volume and 8 out of every 10 in-person payments . As a Nigerian American, I’ve witnessed my father make trips to Western Union to send money back home for decades, and I experienced Nigeria’s fee-laden payment system when visiting the country. Moniepoint is transforming that system. Nnamdi Okike, co-founder and managing partner of 645 Ventures. Moniepoint is not alone. Sea Limited , Grab , Kaspi , Yassir , Nubank 1 — these are companies most Americans have never heard of, despite them being worth several tens or hundreds of billions, following the trail blazed by Tencent , Alibaba and MercadoLibre . These are super apps that bundle banking, commerce, ride-hailing and bill pay into one trusted application. The idea never took hold in the U.S. for one reason: trust is cheap here. With 96% of households already banked , a specialist app inherits the credibility of the financial system. Where trust is cheap, there is no need for a super app. Build trust first In emerging markets, trust is the whole problem. Four conditions tend to precede a super app: High mobile penetration, which makes distribution cheap; weak incumbent competition; poor existing financial services; and the condition most investors screen past, a financial crisis severe enough to strip incumbents of legitimacy. These populations are not merely underbanked. They were harmed, and the institutions that harmed them still hold the market. Brazil froze roughly 80% of bank deposits and financial investments for 18 months in 1990 in an effort to break hyperinflation. The banking consolidation that followed left five banks holding about 80% of banking assets and charging card rates north of 300% . That was the void Nubank was born into. Kazakhstan went through it twice: savings erased by inflation in the thousands of percent when the ruble zone collapsed in 1993, then a 2007–09 banking crisis in which the country’s largest bank, BTA, holding roughly a quarter of the system’s assets, was nationalized and defaulted amid allegations of multibillion-dollar fraud. Kaspi grew into that void. Southeast Asia’s 1997 crisis was harsher still. Indonesia closed 16 banks in a single announcement, the rupiah lost about 85% of its value, and output fell 13 %. Two decades later roughly half of Indonesian adults still had no bank account, which enabled Sea to build Shopee and SeaMoney into that gap. Kaspi also answers the objection I hear most from American investors, which is that these markets are too small to produce large exits. Kazakhstan has only 20 million people, and according to company filings , around 14 million — nearly 70% of its population — use Kaspi. The average user transacts roughly 77 times a month . It earns $9 billion of revenue at 56% EBITDA margins, and its enterprise value is over $17 billion . Depth of spend, not population, sets the ceiling. Compare Nubank to Chime . Nubank has 14x the customers, 127 million to Chime’s 9.5 million , about 7x the revenue and a market capitalization more than 6x larger. Nubank has brought over 31 million previously unbanked Brazilians into the financial system . A technology applied in an overlooked market with a large unaddressed pain point can build a bigger and more defensible company than the same technology applied in a rich one. Screen for the four conditions and a few markets stand out as places where the next super app could emerge: Bangladesh: Five banks looted from the inside for years before the 2024 change in government exposed them , with the government now promising to pay 7.5 million savers whose money is gone. Egypt: Repeated devaluations of the pound between 2016 and 2024, shrinking savings held at banks the state itself owns. Vietnam: Savers pulled 80% of deposits out of one major bank in 2022 after its owner was arrested in a $24 billion fraud. Pakistan: A near-default and 38% inflation in 2023 , then government-built rails and a national ID that makes onboarding nearly costless. One boundary condition: The crisis must be severe enough to delegitimize incumbents but contained enough that the currency and payment rails still work. The first generation of super apps created enormous value for the investors who backed them early. In 2001, the South African media company Naspers paid roughly $34 million for a 46.5% stake in Tencent, a stake later worth more than $100 billion and one of the best tech investments ever made . Sequoia Capital ’s investment in Nubank’s $2 million seed round, combined with its lead Series A investment, was worth $7 billion at the company’s IPO . The second generation is scaling now. The third will be built on stablecoins and AI technologies, in Abidjan, Buenos Aires, Karachi and Lagos, by founders like Tosin Eniolorunda who will play an increasingly important role in the growth of emerging market economies. Nnamdi Okike is co-founder and managing partner of 645 Ventures , where he oversees the firm’s investing strategy, governance and compliance, with a focus on fintech and enterprise technology. Since co-founding 645 Ventures in 2014, he has invested in and partnered with companies including RentSpree , Setpoint , Sequence , Solidus Labs , Order and Uptiq . Previously, he was an investor at Insight Partners , where he invested in 19 companies and had nine exits representing more than $9 billion in exit value. Illustration: Dom Guzman Full disclosure: The author owns shares in Kaspi, Sea Limited and Nubank. None of the companies mentioned are portfolio companies for his firm, 645 Ventures. ↩

payload.text: Brendan Wallace has spent much of the past decade investing in technology that impacts how real estate is bought, built and managed. Now, the Fifth Wall co-founder sees AI changing the kinds of companies worth backing and expanding the definition of proptech itself. Founded in 2016, Los Angeles-based Fifth Wall has grown into one of the largest investment firms focused on real estate technology, with roughly $3 billion in commitments and capital under management. Its portfolio includes Procore , OpenDoor , Blend and Hippo . Notable exits include ServiceTitan , which went public in 2024, and flexible workspace provider Industrious , which real estate giant CBRE took full ownership of in January 2025 at a valuation of more than $800 million. Major real estate and hospitality companies — including CBRE, Hines , Hilton and Marriott — are among its investors, giving the startups it backs a direct connection to potential customers. Wallace, who serves as CEO and chief investment officer, brings experience on both sides of that relationship. He worked in real estate finance at Goldman Sachs and Blackstone before co-founding workforce analytics startup Identified , which was acquired by Workday in 2014, and ridesharing company Cabify . As AI makes certain products easier to replicate, Wallace sees growing potential in startups that use technology to own and operate real estate themselves. In a recent interview with Crunchbase News, we discussed that shift, why proptech funding totals may overlook some of the sector’s biggest investments, what it all means for founders, and the housing problems he believes still need solving. This interview has been lightly edited for brevity and clarity. Crunchbase News: Our recent proptech funding analysis showed capital on pace to roughly match or slightly exceed last year , but across fewer deals. What does that tell you about the market? Brendan Wallace, CEO and chief investment officer of Fifth Wall. (Courtesy photo) Brendan Wallace: My sense is that statistic might belie the actual amount of funding flowing in, because what was previously characterized as proptech in the narrowest sense is probably representing a smaller share of where proptech investors are deploying capital. There are increasingly horizontal solutions that are just as good, if not better, than many of the vertical solutions we’re seeing. We recently made a very big investment out of our growth fund into Higgsfield , the visualization software company. Most people reflexively think of that as being for movies or rendering scenes. But we saw real estate agents and commercial leasing brokers using it to represent spaces. For an unbuilt home, you could feed it blueprints, have it build an entire home, put your family inside and walk through it in a full scene. That had surpassed the industry-specific solutions for space visualization that would have been narrowly defined as proptech. Another category is investment flowing into full-stack businesses: real estate companies themselves. We just invested $135 million into Atoms , and I would be surprised if that fell under the definition of proptech. Those are probably the two categories that might not be captured: horizontal software, with Higgsfield as an example, and businesses that reimagine physical space based on autonomy, AI or robotics. They’re actually building a physical thing. They’re building a real estate company, directly or indirectly. How much is AI driving that shift toward software that serves multiple industries? Wallace: It’s a big part of it. Without something profoundly better that you can’t replicate on your own, there’s less justification for buying outside software. There still is a justification, to be clear. There’s just less of one. No real estate company can build the kind of visualization software Higgsfield has. I don’t believe they ever will. But a tenant engagement app they might have previously purchased and rolled out to their assets, they can now replicate over a long weekend. The imperative to buy these third-party solutions has been reduced, and more value has been placed on the best horizontal solutions, whether that’s a foundation model or a specific use case like sound, audio or visual. I don’t know the statistic, but it would be interesting to know how much real estate companies are spending on foundation models versus proptech applications. If I had to guess, we’re probably close to, or at, an inflection point where it’s passing it. No one would characterize Anthropic as a proptech company, but it might be taking a significant amount of the upstream proptech dollars, and an even larger share downstream once you go through the application layer. Has AI reset the bar for what makes a venture-scale proptech software company? What does a startup need beyond adding AI to existing workflows? Wallace: We’re still figuring that out, but I think it has to be something that can’t be replicated. Anything where the intellectual property moat is not extremely defensible is very challenged, and I think it will be for some time. Simple application point solutions are becoming less financeable by venture investors because the capacity of one of the large labs to build that as an interface, or of a company to build it on its own, has caught up so dramatically. The flip side is that bespoke AI development labs are now building solutions for the real estate industry. We backed one called Antares , which is kind of like a Palantir for real estate. Antares works with a number of our strategic limited partners. They go in-house, identify a problem they think can be solved with an AI-based solution, build the intellectual property specifically for the organization, and leave it with them. It’s more of a fee-for-development model than an intellectual property licensing model. You’re seeing that across industries, and you’re absolutely seeing it in real estate. In some sectors, founders argue that domain expertise gives specialized AI companies an advantage over broad models. How durable do you think that advantage is? Wallace: I’m a little more optimistic about foundation models’ and general intelligence’s capacity to adapt rapidly to specific use cases. I wouldn’t argue that specific legal expertise, for example, is not valuable. But I think that moat collapses over time. You might be on a treadmill. Think about what ChatGPT looked like in 2023 versus what Claude looks like today. At a basic level, it’s the same thing, but they’re totally different things. The sophistication, memory, capacity to be personalized, and ability to build off natural language instructions are unlike anything I think anyone could have anticipated in 2023. What will that look like in 2029? I think what you’re saying is true today. It’s less true than it was, and it might become even less true in three years. Is construction technology still an area of focus for Fifth Wall? Wallace: It is, but it’s less of a focus today. When we look at our performance, it has generally favored two things: pure software businesses, whether marketplaces, consumer software or enterprise software, and full-stack businesses. Anytime you get into physically doing things, the risk profile changes pretty profoundly. I don’t think it should be surprising that construction tech broadly is probably the biggest graveyard in all of venture. Maybe there’s a bigger category, but if there is, it’s not obvious to me. Why do you think construction tech continues to attract significant funding? Wallace: Because it’s still a massive market and a huge problem. If someone can bring greater efficiency to construction, you’re talking about one of the largest markets on earth. It’s such a massive prize that the largest funds are going to focus on it. For founders raising seed or Series A funding, what opportunities would you encourage them to pursue that might not have been fundable a few years ago? Wallace: You can actually build new real estate companies. That hasn’t really been conceptualized as being within a venture mandate, but it’s absolutely something we’d like to see. For example, we have a better approach to buying multifamily assets, stripping out costs, and running more of the processes, operations and management with AI. That’s something I think is eminently fundable today by Fifth Wall and many venture funds. I don’t think that would have been the case five years ago. I’d encourage founders to look at building full-stack, capital-R real estate businesses. The second opportunity is around data. Real estate is characterized by extremely opaque data in a way that’s different from most large financial markets. Nothing that’s happened in proptech in the past 10 years has fundamentally changed that. Where can generative AI provide signal through that opaque data to make capital allocation decisions? Real estate is generally a cash-flowing asset. We don’t necessarily think of it as comparable to bonds or stocks, but it is, and it should be. Can you derive signal by looking at more data or different data, or use generative AI to predict what kind of real estate will perform better? The quantitative model that has existed for securities for a very long time now has the potential to affect real estate, because we have computational capacity that wasn’t previously possible. Are there opportunities you’re interested in that have less to do with AI? Wallace: We’re intrigued by the intersection of land, real estate and the financial instruments around them. To make most of what we describe as real estate, you usually have to build something on land. Land is an input to almost all real estate, but many real estate owners don’t want to own it or take on that risk profile. Is there a way to decouple having to own land from owning and operating a building? That’s less about AI and more about financial engineering. There are new financial solutions emerging in that category that interest us. How could AI, robotics and autonomy change the kinds of real estate businesses founders build? Wallace: I’m interested in entrepreneurs who can conceptualize real estate through a sociological lens: New catalysts are changing how humans use space compared with the past. That’s happened for a long time. E-commerce built the modern industrial real estate industry. Cloud computing, the internet and now AI built the data center industry. Cell towers were born out of mobile phones and smartphone technology. Genome sequencing helped create the lab-space real estate asset class. I think we’re on the precipice of three new catalysts that will spawn entirely new real estate asset classes: AI, robotics and autonomy. In many ways, they’re entangled. Do you expect fewer dedicated proptech venture firms? What would that mean for founders? Wallace: I do think you’re going to see fewer vertical funds, in the narrowest sense of where we started this conversation. Dedicated venture capital funds investing in consumer and enterprise software focused on an industry —– I think you’ll see less of that, and funding will probably continue to go down in that category. The inverse is venture capital funding real estate businesses themselves. I think that’s about to explode. If you were starting a company in this sector today, what problem would you most want to solve? Wallace: Housing drives everything. Housing costs drive our economy, and the U.S. is grappling with a very real housing affordability crisis. It’s unclear how to solve it. There are multiple approaches. One is building homes better, faster and cheaper — that’s construction tech. Another is financing homes at a lower cost. How do you bring efficiency to the housing finance market? That’s a place where we’ve made a lot of money and invested a lot, but I would argue it’s still unsolved. Getting a mortgage is still painful, archaic, slow and too expensive. Related to that is making regulation more efficient to improve housing affordability. That’s not something an entrepreneur can solve alone, but there’s potential to bring efficiency to how cities deal with this problem. There’s an intersection of regulatory technology, policy work and consulting. How do we make it so more people can afford homes in the cities they live in? That problem isn’t going away. Despite everything that’s happened, housing has gotten more expensive, not less. The company previously raised $300 million in a July financing. 4. (tied) Atomic Machines , $250M, micro-manufacturing: Emeryville, California-based Atomic Machines, a startup working on AI-native digital manufacturing systems to build micro-machines directly from code, emerged from stealth and said it has raised $250 million to date from a long list of investors. 7. payload.text: Imagine an insurance company testing two AI assistants. Both understand customer questions, respond naturally and perform well in demonstrations. Six months later, one handles policy renewals inside the insurer’s systems, follows approval rules and escalates exceptions to employees. The other remains a tool people occasionally open. A better model could arrive tomorrow, but replacing the first assistant would require changing how the company operates. That is where I believe an important AI moat is developing: inside customer workflows. Recent acquisitions and partnerships illustrate three implications for founders, investors and boards. Workflow access creates strategic value Schneider Electric ’s agreement to acquire PTC for approximately $22.6 billion in equity value gives it software used to design, manufacture and service physical products, placing it inside customer decisions throughout a product’s lifecycle. Meanwhile, the Synopsys – OpenAI partnership illustrates a similar logic: Combining frontier AI with established chip-design tools and expertise, supported by licensing and revenue sharing. My reading is that these transactions highlight the strategic value of owning the environment in which AI performs useful work. Companies already embedded in complex industries bring customer relationships, domain expertise and trusted processes that AI developers need to commercialize their technology. For founders, that suggests building a position inside a specific customer workflow. For established businesses, it creates an opportunity to turn existing workflow access into bargaining power. Completing recurring work builds defensibility ElevenLabs reported that its agents handle more than 15 million conversations weekly, including refunds, insurance renewals and healthcare bookings, alongside announcing an employee tender at a $22 billion valuation. The operational adoption is particularly relevant to the moat discussion. Once a product connects to internal systems, follows permissions, handles exceptions and reliably completes tasks, replacing it involves migration, testing, retraining and operational risk. This can strengthen retention and create opportunities to serve additional workflows. Integration alone offers limited protection, however. Customers need to depend on the product and measure the value it delivers. Investors should therefore examine how much recurring work flows through the platform, which processes rely on it, and what switching would actually require. Companies can acquire their way into workflows ServiceNow ’s acquisition of Moveworks combines an AI assistant and enterprise search technology with established workflow automation. At completion, Moveworks had 5.5 million employee users, with approximately 250 customers already using both companies’ technologies. The strategic opportunity is to connect employee requests directly to the systems and processes that resolve them across IT, HR and other functions. This creates a clear corp dev agenda: identify the customer workflows the company wants to enter, understand the barriers, and assess whether an acquisition or partnership can accelerate entry. An attractive target may bring technology, customer relationships, integrations and an established role in daily operations. Diligence should test how deeply customers depend on the product, whether those relationships will survive the transaction and whether the combined offering can deliver measurable improvements. As AI capabilities improve, acquiring the right position inside customer operations could become a powerful route to durable growth. payload.text: Gudea has raised $7 million in seed funding to help companies anticipate which online narratives will go viral and understand who is driving them, the startup tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Mudita Venture Partners and Collide Capital co-led the round, bringing the Minneapolis-based startup’s total funding to about $15 million since its 2023 inception, according to co-founder and CEO Keith Presley . The company says its revenue has grown 357% year over year. Its customers include major AI companies and businesses in telecommunications, entertainment and retail, although it declined to identify them, citing the sensitive nature of its work. Gudea’s premise is that tracking mentions and hashtags tells companies only part of the story. The startup aims to map how information moves across people, groups and platforms, then predict how far a narrative will spread, when it will take off, and when it will fade. Presley describes Gudea as the “storm tracker for the internet.” “As a meteorologist uses patterns to predict the weather, we’re using patterns to predict information,” he said in an interview, adding that the startup covers over 600 social media platforms. From disrupting disinformation to tracking brands Gudea’s management team, from left: Matt Chase, Jonathan Sperber, James Thomin, Georgia Paul and Keith Presley. (Courtesy photo) The business grew out of the George Washington Initiative, a nonprofit that adapted tactics used by the intelligence community to disrupt online Al Qaeda and ISIS networks for domestic information campaigns. The team initially searched for existing software that could show how information traveled, but found social listening tools insufficient. James Thomin , Gudea’s CTO and one of its founders, began working on technology to map those pathways. When the team examined the backlash around Bud Light’s marketing campaign with actor Dylan Mulvaney, it reached a turning point. The campaign’s critics used the same information pathways that had carried COVID disinformation, noted Presley. The team realized “that these patterns were repeating, and that there was a much broader use case,” he recalled. The technology spun out into a company in 2023. Its initial commercial focus has been reputational risk management, which entails helping large businesses spot potentially consequential stories before they spread widely. “We don’t need to know what we’re looking for to find it, so we can find all of those good or bad narratives before you know what keywords you should be searching for,” Presley said. Who’s driving the conversation? One way Gudea operates is by assessing whether users or accounts exhibiting unusual behavior are driving online conversations. It also examines how narratives move from less visible online communities into more mainstream platforms. For example, the startup conducted an analysis of online claims linking Taylor Swift to Nazism around an album release. 1 Georgia Paul , Gudea’s director of client experience, told Crunchbase News that the analysis uncovered that the narrative was being manipulated. The company says its work has also involved cases of corporate espionage and stock market manipulation. More recently, it has been examining how conversations about data centers affect businesses in AI and energy. Its technology can also identify positive trends companies might capitalize on, according to Paul, in addition to reputational threats. Predicting what spreads next Gudea uses deep learning, including graph neural networks, to analyze behavior, and uses a large language model to summarize findings. “Those behavior patterns are like fingerprints, and so our AI then recognizes those fingerprints, pulls it out, and then we use an LLM to summarize,” Presley said. The company sells its software to businesses through offerings that include alerts, platform access and automatically delivered reports. The latter emerged from its work with senior teams that were unlikely to log into a platform themselves. Presley cited Blackbird , Cyabra and Alethea as competitors in narrative intelligence, while positioning Gudea’s predictions as its distinguishing feature. Gudea tells customers “how long till it goes viral, how many people will be impacted, and how long till it goes away,” he said. For Gudea, the broader aim remains connected to its nonprofit origins: making the mechanisms behind online information more visible. “People are making real-world decisions off of what they see online, and not all of that information is authentic,” Presley said. The startup plans to use its new capital to expand its team, develop new features and broaden its coverage across platforms, languages and regions. It currently has 39 customers and approximately 25 employees. Buddy Foster , investor at Mudita Venture Partners, notes that AI is changing how stories are spread on the internet. “Damage to a brand is now starting in the fringe parts of the internet and builds momentum before it ever reaches a headline. It’s a big problem,” he wrote via email. “Gudea has built a solution that has the potential to own the market and know more than just the headlines. They can really see what is coming before it’s a problem.” Most other tools on the market are “reactive and surface-layer,” in Foster’s view, whereas Gudea is more proactive. “Gudea models how information moves across the internet and hundreds of platforms, so it can spot a problem before anyone knows to search for it,” he added. “Since it looks at behavior instead of content, its ability to be proactive gets better even as the internet gets more clouded.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To AI Startups In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman Clarification: The co-lead investors in the article were updated. Gudea conducted that research for press coverage rather than for Swift, who was not a client. ↩

payload.text: In Q3, Europe posted its strongest venture funding quarter in four years, with AI companies driving those gains, Crunchbase data shows. European startup funding reached $25 billion last quarter, well above the $14 billion invested in Q3 2025 and up slightly from the $24 billion invested in Q2. Quarterly funding was up 77% year over year, per Crunchbase data. While the U.K. continued to lead startup funding totals last quarter, Germany and France both posted their strongest quarters since the boom years of 2021 and early 2022. Last quarter’s funding totals were boosted heavily by a $3.5 billion investment in Paris-based Mistral , the largest venture round ever for a Europe-based company. Table of contents Billion-dollar fundings Venture expands beyond the UK Late-stage rise Early stage Seed Looking forward Methodology Glossary of funding terms Billion-dollar fundings Four European companies raised billion-dollar-plus fundings, representing close to 40% of the region’s startup capital raised last quarter. They include Mistral, which also announced its new open-source model Large 4, an LLM it claims outperforms competing open source models on several vectors. Data center provider Nscale raised a convertible note of $3.36 billion that it says it will convert once it goes public, which it has filed plans to do. Two defense tech startups also raised billion-dollar-plus rounds last quarter: Helsing raised a Series E of $1.8 billion, and Quantum Systems raised $1.2 billion. AI drove 75% of European funding this past quarter — totaling $18.8 billion — the highest proportion on record. Investments in physical tech in Europe in defense, data centers, energy, aerospace and robotics accounted for roughly half of European funding in Q3. Venture expands beyond the UK The U.K. led the region’s quarterly funding totals with $7.5 billion even as Germany and France gained market share for venture capital funding in Q3 with $5 billion and $4.8 billion invested, respectively. The fourth-largest market, Sweden, saw $1.5 billion in venture capital invested while the Netherlands and Spain posted their strongest quarter since the COVID boom years with $1.4 billion and $1.2 billion invested in their startup markets, respectively. Late-stage rise A total of $17.3 billion — 70% of Europe’s Q3 venture capital — was invested in late-stage deals in 83 companies. Outside of the billion-dollar rounds, large late-stage fundings between $400 million to $700 million were raised by Stockholm-based health scanning provider Neko Health ; Lisbon-based autonomous drone developer Tekever ; Spain-based Multiverse Computing , which offers model compression technology for enterprise AI adoption; Amsterdam-based AI deployment startup Wonderful ; Bayern-based space transportation company The Exploration Co. ; and Stockholm-based AI web application builder Lovable . Early stage Europe’s early-stage funding totaled $5.7 billion into just over 200 companies in Q3, down quarter over quarter and flat year over year. The largest Series A funding deals, each $200 million or over, were raised by Eindhoven-based AI semiconductor startup Euclyd and Zürich-based autonomous construction company Gravis Robotics . Large Series B rounds were raised by Munich-based fusion energy company Proxima Fusion and London-based optical computing provider Olix . Seed Europe’s seed funding fell quarter over quarter and was flat year over year. Around $2 billion was invested in more than 750 companies at seed stage in Q3. London-based managed inference company Callosum raised the largest seed round at $100 million, followed by Munich-based AI for robotics startup Microagi , which raised $55 million. Looking forward Europe’s momentum in 2026 continued in Q3, which was the second quarter this year when venture totals topped $20 billion. Those are figures not seen in the region’s startup scene since Q3 2022. Along with growth in AI funding, late-stage funding noticeably increased last quarter with many of the leading rounds sourced across multiple European countries. Europe represented 16% of global venture capital in Q3 , although the true impact of its technology and startups is higher, with many of the region’s startups expanding or moving to the U.S. to capitalize on the rapid growth of AI there. At the same time, Europe’s ambition to build leading deep-tech companies and meet demand for sovereign AI will be tested in the quarters ahead by its ability to mobilize the substantial capital these businesses need. Related Crunchbase queries: Europe Venture Funding In 2026 European M&A In 2026 For Venture-Backed Companies Related reading: Crunchbase Data: Q3 2026 Posted A Record Count Of Billion-Dollar Rounds As The Global AI Race Heats Up Reporter’s Notebook: Europe’s Sovereign AI Push Needs Customers As Well As Capital Methodology The data contained in this report comes directly from Crunchbase, and is based on reported data. Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. Glossary of funding terms Seed and angel consists of seed, pre-seed and angel rounds. Crunchbase also includes venture rounds of unknown series, equity crowdfunding and convertible notes at $3 million (USD or as-converted USD equivalent) or less. Early-stage consists of Series A and Series B rounds, as well as other round types. Crunchbase includes venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $3 million, and those less than or equal to $15 million. Late-stage consists of Series C, Series D, Series E and later-lettered venture rounds following the “Series [Letter]” naming convention. Also included are venture rounds of unknown series, corporate venture and other rounds above $15 million. Corporate rounds are only included if a company has raised an equity funding at seed through a venture series funding round. Technology growth is a private-equity round raised by a company that has previously raised a “venture” round. (So basically, any round from the previously defined stages.) Illustration: Dom Guzman

目前已经开放登录、积分购买、生成、私有结果播放和下载。Standard 720p、12 秒的一次生成消耗 10 积分；生成或交付确认失败时会退回本次消耗的积分。生成时间会受模型和队列影响，不承诺固定时长。

我现在主要想听听大家对两个问题的反馈：
1. 两张照片的准备说明是否够清楚；
2. 场景和 Prompt 设置有没有让人不知道怎么选的地方。

网站： https://thehotellobbyai.com/
使用说明： https://thehotellobbyai.com/how-it-works

说明：我是这个工具的制作者。

title: Media
summary:
今天 **Gemini-4-Argon** 正式发布了，实测它的长程规划和调度决策能力强得让人后背发凉。
既然模型大脑已经到了这个水位，再拿它当「聊天框里的个人助理」就太浪费了。

我决定做一个为期 **7 天** 的公开实验：
**给 Gemini 4 配齐一台 Mac 电脑、一个独立浏览器、一台专属手机，再配一群 DeepSeek 驱动的 AI 员工，让它替我运营一家软件公司。目标只有一个：7 天内从零做出一款知名付费软件的替代品，并直接免费开源。**

![电脑与手机设备实拍图]( https://media.munk.sh/blog/day-01/machines.jpg)

---

## 一、1,000 美金预算：Gemini 当高管，DeepSeek 当员工

跑多 Agent 最怕两件事：全用旗舰模型，两天烧穿预算；全用便宜模型，规划一团乱麻。
这次实验里，我用自己写的本地运行时（**Munk AI**），把 **$1,000 美金 Token** 拆成了高低两档：

- **800 美金给 Gemini 4 （公司高管 / 总架构师 / 主力研发）**
  负责守住公司全局记忆、拆解产品需求、攻坚核心代码、制定验收标准，并在关键路口向我的手机发请示。
- **200 美金给 DeepSeek （高频专项员工：实机自测 + 新媒体运营）**
  - **跑实机自测**：桌面与手机 UI 验收要连续跑几十轮「看界面 → 点按钮 → 验状态」，非常吃上下文。底层把控件和 OCR 坐标算好后，交给 DeepSeek 跑既快又省钱，测出 Bug 立刻打回给 Gemini 修；
  - **跑全网运营**：负责生成小红书配图、用脚本与 FFmpeg 剪辑宣传视频、再控制浏览器去各平台发帖和评论区互动。

![Agent 设置页面截图]( https://media.munk.sh/blog/day-01/agents.png)

---

## 二、真手真脚：不止会写代码

光会写代码那叫 IDE 插件，不叫软件公司。我交给了这家 AI 公司三样物理工具：

1. **直接操控 Mac 电脑（ Computer Use ）**：就算原生桌面软件没有 API ，它也能直接看懂屏幕界面、识别按钮并自己点按操作。
2. **独立浏览器 + 专属实体手机**：浏览器用来查竞品、看文档、去各平台发帖回评论；桌边配给它的实体手机不仅能测 App ，后续连收手机验证码都能自己搞定。
3. **自测硬闸**：代码写完必须过编译和实机点按自测，不过不准合入主线。

---

## 三、7 天实验的死规矩

1. **我不写一行代码，不手动发一条帖子**。
2. **我只负责「手机审批」+「填密码/付款辅助」**：关键节点我在手机上点「同意 / 驳回」；遇到首次平台登录或付款时，它呼叫我搭把手（密码绝不进 AI 上下文），登完它继续自己跑。
3. **第 7 天交卷**：不管最终完成度是 80% 还是 100%，**做出来的替代软件直接免费开源**，同时把背后这家 AI 公司的配置与 Munk AI 开放出来给大家体验。

![飞书手机审批：Munk AI 机器人叫我完成 GitHub 登录]( https://media.munk.sh/blog/day-01/feishu.jpg)

---

## 四、Day 1 / 7：做什么产品，让 Gemini 4 自己调研、决定

今天（ 10 月 14 日）是 **Day 1 / 7**。
具体平替哪一款付费软件，我都没有直接定，而是交给了 Gemini 4 自己调研、决定。

我今天给 Gemini 4 下达的第 1 个总目标是：**派员工用浏览器去全网调研目前收费贵、呼声高、但还没有公认开源替代品的软件，开一场内部圆桌评估，今晚之前把前 3 个备选立项方案发到我手机上等我拍板。**

大家平时有什么「明明功能简单、却非要收高价买断或订阅」的怨念软件？**欢迎在评论区提名！** 我会让 AI 员工去抓评论区的高赞提名一起纳入评估，明天 **Day 2** 正式揭晓最终选定的目标软件并开工写代码！

title: Github
summary:
新人第一次发帖。

地址： https://github.com/LingCore/WinShun

这是啥：类似 everything 与 listary 的程序
本程序 10 月 8 刚上线，有很多问题请大家体谅，我天天在更新，很多地方已经七七八八了。

更新好几天，说下感受吧，最主要是就是一个字“累”，累死我了（ opus 和 fable 也快累死了），几天改了超多需求，优化了超多体验，修复了超多 bug ；但是结果是好的，工具对我而言越来越满意了，虽然还有些没有做，但是我相信我能做到 TOP1 ，只做最好。

有建议欢迎反馈，觉得好用就给个 Star 吧！您的支持是我更新的最大动力！
star 越多我越爽
:smiling_face_with_three_hearts:

Windows 上的搜索小工具「 Win 顺」，连按两下 Ctrl 就能搜，边打字边出结果。Everything 和 Listary 的活，它一个全干了。

能搜什么

文件、文件夹：三百多万个文件，几毫秒出结果，新建、改名的文件马上就能搜到； NAS 、别的电脑上的共享文件夹也能一起搜
按类型找：选中“文件”后，下面一排文件夹、文档、图片、视频、压缩包……按 Shift+Tab 切换，也能自己加类型
文件里的字：Word 、Excel 、PPT 、PDF 、WPS 、代码都能搜，直接告诉你在第几行、第几页；词后面加 文件夹名/ 就只搜那个文件夹，比如 第三季度销售额 财务/
按意思找：记不得原词也能找，? 去年报销的规定 就能找到写着“差旅费用申请”的文档（插件，默认关，模型用本机的 Ollama 或你自己的密钥）
软件：微软商店装的也能搜到，打 vsc 就出 VS Code
系统设置：打“网卡”直接出网络连接，不用一层层点
网页：打 zhihu 显卡 就在知乎上搜，自带百度、B 站、小红书、京东等十个常用网站
全都支持拼音，打 ndbg 就能找到“年度报告”；打错了同音字（年度报高）也能按读音找到。每行图标上标着序号，Ctrl+1 ～ Ctrl+9 直接打开，不用先按住 Ctrl 。

不只是搜索

资源管理器里：双击文件夹空白处，弹出收藏的、最近的、别的窗口开着的文件夹，选一个当前窗口就转过去；右键“用 Win 顺 搜索此处”，只在这个文件夹里搜
“打开”“另存为”窗口：旁边多一个搜索框，搜到直接跳过去； Ctrl+G 跳到资源管理器正开着的文件夹；也可以设成自动转过去：对话框一出现就转，或者从资源管理器切回来时再转
剪贴板历史：可以代替 Win+V ，字、图片、文件都能找回来，弹在光标那一行下面； Alt+1 ～ Alt+9 直接粘贴第几条；图片里的字也能搜，还能选中复制；固定的可以排在最前，也能自己排顺序
任务栏搜索框：可以代替 Windows 自带的搜索，能放在开始按钮右边（和系统自带的搜索框位置一样），Win+S 也能打开
收藏夹：常去的文件夹起个关键字，一打就开
插件：= 1+2*3 算数、12 inch to cm 换算、kill 结束进程，也能自己写
AI 助手：Claude 、Cursor 、VS Code 一键连上，让 AI 帮你找文件（默认只读）
玩游戏时双击 Ctrl 不会弹出来，不会打断你蹲下。

Qt 6 + C++20 ，用的时候内存一两百 MB ，放着不用很快降到十几 MB 。平时用普通权限运行，开机、打开都不弹 UAC 。免费开源（ MIT ），不用注册；除了检查更新、取网站图标，以及你自己打开的“按意思找”云模型，都不联网。支持 Win10 （ 1809 及以上，含 LTSC ）/ Win11 64 位，有安装版，也有解压就能用的免安装版（数据都存在旁边的 data 文件夹里，整个拷走就行）。

本程序 10 月 8 刚上线，有很多问题请大家体谅，我天天在更新，很多地方已经七七八八了。

更新好几天，说下感受吧，最主要是就是一个字“累”，累死我了（ opus 和 fable 也快累死了），几天改了超多需求，优化了超多体验，修复了超多 bug ；但是结果是好的，工具对我而言越来越满意了，虽然还有些没有做，但是我相信我能做到 TOP1 ，只做最好。

有建议欢迎反馈，觉得好用就给个 Star 吧！您的支持是我更新的最大动力！
star 越多我越爽
:smiling_face_with_three_hearts:

Windows 上的搜索小工具「 Win 顺」，连按两下 Ctrl 就能搜，边打字边出结果。Everything 和 Listary 的活，它一个全干了。

能搜什么

文件、文件夹：三百多万个文件，几毫秒出结果，新建、改名的文件马上就能搜到； NAS 、别的电脑上的共享文件夹也能一起搜
按类型找：选中“文件”后，下面一排文件夹、文档、图片、视频、压缩包……按 Shift+Tab 切换，也能自己加类型
文件里的字：Word 、Excel 、PPT 、PDF 、WPS 、代码都能搜，直接告诉你在第几行、第几页；词后面加 文件夹名/ 就只搜那个文件夹，比如 第三季度销售额 财务/
按意思找：记不得原词也能找，? 去年报销的规定 就能找到写着“差旅费用申请”的文档（插件，默认关，模型用本机的 Ollama 或你自己的密钥）
软件：微软商店装的也能搜到，打 vsc 就出 VS Code
系统设置：打“网卡”直接出网络连接，不用一层层点
网页：打 zhihu 显卡 就在知乎上搜，自带百度、B 站、小红书、京东等十个常用网站
全都支持拼音，打 ndbg 就能找到“年度报告”；打错了同音字（年度报高）也能按读音找到。每行图标上标着序号，Ctrl+1 ～ Ctrl+9 直接打开，不用先按住 Ctrl 。

不只是搜索

资源管理器里：双击文件夹空白处，弹出收藏的、最近的、别的窗口开着的文件夹，选一个当前窗口就转过去；右键“用 Win 顺 搜索此处”，只在这个文件夹里搜
“打开”“另存为”窗口：旁边多一个搜索框，搜到直接跳过去； Ctrl+G 跳到资源管理器正开着的文件夹；也可以设成自动转过去：对话框一出现就转，或者从资源管理器切回来时再转
剪贴板历史：可以代替 Win+V ，字、图片、文件都能找回来，弹在光标那一行下面； Alt+1 ～ Alt+9 直接粘贴第几条；图片里的字也能搜，还能选中复制；固定的可以排在最前，也能自己排顺序
任务栏搜索框：可以代替 Windows 自带的搜索，能放在开始按钮右边（和系统自带的搜索框位置一样），Win+S 也能打开
收藏夹：常去的文件夹起个关键字，一打就开
插件：= 1+2*3 算数、12 inch to cm 换算、kill 结束进程，也能自己写
AI 助手：Claude 、Cursor 、VS Code 一键连上，让 AI 帮你找文件（默认只读）
玩游戏时双击 Ctrl 不会弹出来，不会打断你蹲下。

Qt 6 + C++20 ，用的时候内存一两百 MB ，放着不用很快降到十几 MB 。平时用普通权限运行，开机、打开都不弹 UAC 。免费开源（ MIT ），不用注册；除了检查更新、取网站图标，以及你自己打开的“按意思找”云模型，都不联网。支持 Win10 （ 1809 及以上，含 LTSC ）/ Win11 64 位，有安装版，也有解压就能用的免安装版（数据都存在旁边的 data 文件夹里，整个拷走就行）。

title: Petal
summary: open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free

extra.author: thedracle
extra.original_title: Show HN: Petal, open-source CoScreen/ScreenHero finally free

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I’m Jason Thomas, one of the founders of CoScreen.

As some of you may know, Datadog sunset the CoScreen service on July 31st.

Four of us from the original CoScreen team have spent the last couple months building a free and open source pair programming tool inspired by those that came before us: It’s called Petal (https://github.com/kiruna-labs/petal)

Some history first, because when we started CoScreen we had hoped to break the sad and established pattern of this industry.

Screenhero was an exceptional tool that a lot of us loved for pairing. Multiple cursors, low latency, you could click your partner’s editor, and just start typing. It felt like magic while we had it. Then Slack bought it in 2015, and shut down the standalone app in December 2017.

When Till, Max, and I started CoScreen, we were aware of this history, and wanted to build an even more magical collaboration and screen sharing experience: the entire concept was “throw a window from your laptop up on someone else’s screen, and start collaborating with zero friction.”

Datadog acquired us in 2022, and thus began the great adventure of adapting our real-time technology into Datadog products, while also continue developing CoScreen as a standalone tool from the Datadog ecosystem. Datadog invested in the product for years and we’re thankful for that. But CoScreen itself proved, like so many other screen sharing tool acquisitions, to be too tangential from the customer base and core mission. We instead built other communication features in Datadog, the integrations with other video platforms, and also its wildly successful MCP server. We weren't the only ones. Around was bought by Miro and shut down in March 2025. Multi (formerly Remotion) was acqui-hired by OpenAI in 2024 and shut down about a month later. It's nearly always the same story: a small team builds something hard that people love, a platform buys it for the team or the feature, and the standalone product doesn't survive the integration. So we decided firmly to do things differently this time. Petal is completely free and open source and we aren't monetizing it. If we lose interest or get hit by a bus, you can self-host it or fork it, and nobody can sunset it on you. Honestly it's a love letter to everyone in this community that supported us, believed in us, and to liberate collaborative screen sharing from this vicious cycle.

We hope through this we can help foster a large and vibrant community around innovating in this product sector. What Petal does: shared windows show up as real windows on your desktop, movable and resizable, not tiles in a grid. Several people can share at once, everyone gets a labeled cursor, and you can click into any shared window to type and scroll. Rooms are persistent, so you click once to join "eng-sync" instead of passing links around. It runs on macOS and Windows (Linux is next, this time for real and you can help us!), plus a web app. Media goes over LiveKit. You can use our hosted instance with zero config, or point the app at your own LiveKit server with one docker-compose if you want the traffic to stay on your network or even use an entirely different video backend if you want to. The part that still feels strange to us: CoScreen took almost six years to build. The first version of Petal took under eight weeks, from scratch, with frontier models like Fable and Astra doing a lot of the work. Real-time video and window capture is some of the most unforgiving code we have ever written, so we didn't expect that. We will do a proper writeup on what worked and what didn't, and are happy to answer questions about it here. Till, Darren, Max and I will be in the thread.

title: clova
summary: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox

extra.author: edpin2000
extra.original_title: Show HN: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox

story_text.value:
Infinite inboxes, including prefixes where you don't have to create inboxes before you use them -- they self create when you add a suffix.

Three types of inboxes: - One sender. Locks to the first domain to send email (except gmail, outlook, etc where it locks to an email account for obivous reasons. It bounces everyone else. - Temporary. Lasts for a while (24h, 7days, etc) then bounces. Received messages stay or go as per your choice. - Prefix. The most powerful. Declare a prefix like "service" and then invent any suffix, like "service-netflix" or "service$bank" and it creates a new one-sender inbox locked to whoever wrote first.

Bring you own domain. Bring your own AI (MCP server ready). Forwarding.

Please help me test it.

title: T0
summary: We trained a 256M SOTA open-weights time-series forecasting model

extra.author: LTMeyer
extra.original_title: Show HN: T0: We trained a 256M SOTA open-weights time-series forecasting model

story_text.value:
Hi everyone, we are excited to share t0-gamma, the latest model in our t0 family. It is a 256M parameter open-weights foundation model for time series (TSFM). It runs on CPU, GPU or Apple chips.

https://huggingface.co/theforecastingcompany/t0-gamma

t0 leverages historical data to forecast the likely outcomes over a given horizon. It does so zero-shot. It works on almost any time series, as it can pick up small signals like trends and seasonality. It can also leverage future-known information, like holidays, promotions and weather forecasts. Under the hood, t0 is a transformer that alternates attention between time and across the variates of a series.

t0 is agnostic to the domain and to the frequency of the time series. For instance, it can be used to predict retail or electricity demand, as well as server metrics.

On European day ahead electricity prices, t0 reduces the error by a third compared with a naive baseline that repeats the previous day. Adding weather forecasts or holiday information improves it even further. There is a Colab notebook to try it. t0 has also been tested independently on electricity prices in Texas (ERCOT).

https://colab.research.google.com/github/theforecastingcompa...

Like other TSFMs, t0 outperforms classical techniques such as ARIMA, ETS and their variants. On the public benchmarks GIFT-Eval, fev-bench and TIME, t0-gamma currently ranks first among the other TSFMs. It means it is the most accurate model there is to date. Like other TSFMs, t0 can be used inside agentic, routing or ensembling systems. This can improve the scores on the leaderboards even further. Our tech report describes the model family and its evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24559

Trying it takes a few Python lines.

  pip install "tfc-t0[torch]>=0.6.0"

  from t0 import T0Forecaster
  model = T0Forecaster.from_pretrained("theforecastingcompany/t0-gamma").eval()
  history = ...  # history of the time series to predict
  out = model.predict(history, horizon=24)
  out.median
There is more to come. We are working to extend t0 to joint forecasts across related series and hierarchies, much longer contexts and faster inference.

Please give it a try, and don't hesitate to tell us where it works and where it doesn't.

We are The Forecasting Company. We want to help companies reduce their uncertainty about the future, so they can make better decisions. We are starting our journey by building foundation models for time series.

title: Geneva
summary: a Rust FFmpeg CLI alternative with HTML/CSS graphics

extra.author: fbnt
extra.original_title: Show HN: Geneva, a Rust FFmpeg CLI alternative with HTML/CSS graphics

story_text.value:
I built this for my own use case, and I think other people could benefit from it.

It's essentially a Rust rewrite of the ffmpeg CLI command, but with a modern API and good defaults + a native HTML/CSS composition engine that's been fine tuned for speed and memory efficiency. Under the hood, it still uses the libav* codecs from ffmpeg, so it can still work on a variety of formats.

Works very well with AI agents too: prompt what kind or intro/animation/graphics you need (or give it a reference), let the LLM come up with the HTML/CSS for it (Opus 5.5 is quite good at this), and let it use them on geneva.

It's way faster than the usual alternatives for putting still or animated graphics on videos (remotion, playwright etc.) because it doesn't use a browser or chromium. Everything is rendered natively, in a single pass.

title: museumofages
summary: A guided 3D Leonardo da Vinci museum, built in code

extra.author: micstradev
extra.original_title: Show HN: A guided 3D Leonardo da Vinci museum, built in code

story_text.value:
Hello HN,

I am the founder of a small nonprofit which built Museum of Ages. We opened its first wing last week, a digital Leonardo da Vinci museum. It is a virtual tour with 17 stops, his works and then his last house in Amboise. The entrance is free.

At the different stops you can see for example his paintings close to their real size, or 15 of his machines rebuilt in code, and you can have a look at 29 of his anatomy sheets. We also selected 207 of his manuscript pages which you can read in a virtual reading table, mirror the view to read his writing and 131 of the 207 are translated. We also rebuilt his last house in Amboise on the later stops of the walk. The museum is available in seven languages.

Each stop has one of four grades as a label, documented, reconstructed, conjectural and not known. In a detailed view the user can have a closer look at the sources.

The materials of the rooms and machines are created in Three.js. The museum runs with WebGPU. If the browser doesn’t support it, the fallback is WebGL2. To create the textures we used Creative Commons Zero photo scans (CC0) and for a few small objects we use free 3D models (CC0).

Our mission is to create digital museums you can walk as not everyone can get to a museum, because illness or disability keeps them away. Some cannot afford the trip or just reside far away. So our goal is also to make our digital museums as accessible as possible. Therefore we also pre-rendered the walk so that it also works on older phones and is easy to use for older people.

We released the code under AGPL-3.0. The texts and pictures are CC BY-SA 4.0. Reproductions have their own licenses. https://github.com/chipmates/museumofages

We put a lot of time and passion into the museum and hope you like it. We are happy about any feedback. Which digital museum would you like to see next?
